OBITUARY ELEANOR ELLIS (nee Jones) Eleanor passed away peacefully September I at home with her family at her side, following a brief illness from lung cancer. She was born February 22, 1915 in Glovcrsville, New York and spent her early years there. She graduated from Smith College, Northampton, Masachusetts, and worked for several years in New York City before joining the American Red Cross. She served in Great Britain and Europe for two years during World War 11 and was awarded the Bronze Star and the Medal of Freedom. While stationed in Germany, she met Glenn Ellis, a Flight Lieutenant in the Royal Canadian Air Force. They were married in Gloversville on December 28, 1946 and she moved to Canada with him. In 1951, they moved to Town of Mt. Royal and began raising their two daughters. In 1961, they moved to Glens Falls, New York, later returning to Montreal. In 1968, they founded Sesame Industries LTD, a manufacturer and marketer of unique tapes for the packaging industry, located in St. Andre est, Quebec. Eleanor was Vice-president and Secretary -Treasurer of the Company. For twenty-one years they enjoyed a country home in nearby Carillon. In 1985, they sold the family business to H.B. Fuller Co. which continued to operate in St. Andre est until Fuller closed the factory in December 2003. Eleanor had an energetic zest for life, and a generous spirit. She was an active volunteer for many years for the Mayeourt Club in Montreal, the Unitarian Church in Montreal and Amnesty International, reflecting her passionate beliefs in human rights. Her thirst for knowledge and abundant curiosity made her an avid reader and lifelong lifelong learner and a regular attendant at courses, lectures, concerts and plays. From an early age, travel was one of Eleanor's chief delights and she visited doens of countries in her lifetime. Eleanor was a longtime subscriber to, and supporter of, several of Montreal's cultural institutions: the Montreal Symphony, the Centaur Theatre and Les Grands Ballets Canadiens. She was also an advocate for social environmental causes - writing letters for years on behalf of Amnesty International, supporting Greenpeace since it opened its doors and advocating recycling in her condominium. She is greatly missed by Glenn, their daughters Jacqueline of Portsmouth, New Hampshire and Antoinette (Toni) of Flora, Ontario and their five grandchildren: Lynn, Brian, Amie Vaccaro of Portsmouth and Joshua and Benjamin Taylor of Elora. The partners made a bold move back in 1976 when many in the jittery anglo community began the exodus along Highway 401 to Toronto and points beyond. Rather than joining the stampede, the two entrepreneurs staked a claim to a shopping mall on St. John's Blvd. in Pointe Claire, near the highway In the wake of the election of the Parti Quebecois government and its avowed goal of independence, it was an immense risk for Johnston and Scheunert. They plunked down their money and snapped up the strip mall, one of the earliest and one of the largest in Quebec when it was built in the 1950s, from the Steinberg family's Ivanhoe real-estate wing. The Steinberg's supermarket supermarket anchored the mall at the northwest corner. While the partners won't discuss numbers, it is safe to say they bought the mall for a rock-bottom price because because that's where real estate was in those days and where it languished for many years after. But in the face of political turbulence, turbulence, the revolution in retailing with the advent of the big-box stores, giant shopping centres, megacentres and fashion centres, Plaza Pointe Claire, as it is now known, has grown, innovated and grown some more. As new indoor malls were built, Scheunert and Johnston enclosed theirs and built space for more stores. As the population aged, they built a second storey to add offices for doctor's and medical labs. As homeowners began began cocooning, they built an expansion expansion on the southern end to house a garden centre. Bombardier Inc. chief executive executive Paul Tellier tried unsuccessfully last year to persuade chairperson Laurent Beaudoin to collapse the company's company's dual-class share structure into a one-share, one-vote setup. Tellier rightly saw abolition of the share structure as a stepping stone for Bombardier to obtain a listing on the New York Stock Exchange and access to a new audience of deep-pocketed U.S. investors. But the move was too much for Beaudoin and the Bombardier family to swallow. They control the company by virtue of Class A shares that carry 10 votes for every one vote carried by the Class B shares. The family couldn't face giving up control, so Bombardier remains remains off the BH( Board.
